title: Tribunal Clears Lalit Modi in IPL 2009 FEMA Case, Paving Way for India Return After 16 Years
excerpt: The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal has set aside the Enforcement Directorate's penalties against the former IPL commissioner, ruling that the 2009 tournament remittances were current account transactions that did not require RBI approval.
body:
• The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal set aside all penalties imposed on Lalit Modi by the Enforcement Directorate in the IPL 2009 FEMA case, ruling that the foreign remittances were current account transactions.
  • The tribunal found Modi was neither responsible for BCCI's statutory FEMA compliance nor vested with the financial authority alleged by the ED.
  • Modi has indicated he plans to return to India by late 2026 or early 2027, after his daughter's baby is born in October.
  • Penalties on former BCCI officials were also reduced — N. Srinivasan's from ₹1 crore to ₹10 lakh, and the BCCI's from ₹4 crore to ₹1 crore.

Former IPL chairman Lalit Modi has been cleared of the principal charges in the FEMA case stemming from the 2009 Indian Premier League season held in South Africa, closing what he called "the single most significant legal matter" from that era and opening the door to his return to India after 16 years abroad.

What the Tribunal Ruled

The Appellate Tribunal under the Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators Act (SAFEMA) delivered its verdict on 16 July, overturning the Enforcement Directorate's core contention that the BCCI's remittances to South Africa for IPL 2009 constituted capital account transactions requiring prior Reserve Bank of India approval.

https://x.com/CNBCTV18News/status/2079929462670725238

In its 105-page order, the tribunal held that the principal foreign remittances — approximately ₹243.45 crore ($4.98 million at the time) transferred to organise the tournament in South Africa — were current account transactions. This distinction is critical: current account transactions under FEMA generally do not require prior RBI clearance, while capital account transactions do.

The tribunal also found that Modi "was neither responsible for BCCI's statutory FEMA compliance nor vested with the financial authority alleged by the Enforcement Directorate," effectively dismantling both pillars of the ED's case against him, according to Cricbuzz.

"For over sixteen years I have consistently maintained one simple position: I acted in good faith, in the best interests of Indian cricket and the IPL, and committed no personal wrongdoing."

— Lalit Modi, Former IPL Chairman

Background: Why IPL 2009 Moved to South Africa

The second season of the IPL was shifted from India to South Africa in 2009 because the tournament's dates clashed with India's general elections, making it impossible to provide adequate security at venues across the country. Modi, then IPL commissioner, oversaw the relocation.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=tAtMdIEyww8

The ED subsequently alleged that the BCCI had transferred funds abroad without proper authorisation, issuing show-cause notices in 2011. In 2018, the adjudicating authority imposed penalties across six notices totalling ₹10.65 crore on Modi, along with separate penalties on former BCCI secretary N. Srinivasan, former treasurer Pandove, and the BCCI itself.

Modi challenged the penalties through six separate appeals before the tribunal.

Penalties Reduced for BCCI Officials

While the tribunal cleared Modi of the principal charges, it upheld two findings against the BCCI: that the board had remitted a higher amount than recorded in its books and that there was a delay in repatriating ticket sale proceeds to India.

However, penalties were sharply reduced. Srinivasan's penalty was cut from ₹1 crore to ₹10 lakh, Pandove's from ₹50 lakh to ₹5 lakh, and the BCCI's from ₹4 crore to ₹1 crore, according to CricketAddictor.

Plans for Return

Following the ruling, Modi told media that the decision had cleared the way for his return to India. He said he expects to come back by late 2026 or early 2027, adding that his daughter is expecting a baby in October and he plans to return after the birth.

Modi has lived abroad for more than a decade, with various legal proceedings and investigations keeping him away from India. The FEMA case was the most significant of these, and its resolution removes a major legal overhang.

"The successful staging of that season ensured that the IPL survived and ultimately became one of the world's most valuable sporting properties," Modi said, defending the 2009 decision that triggered the entire legal saga.

What's Next

The verdict marks a turning point for Modi's long-running legal battles, though it remains to be seen whether his return will revive any role in Indian cricket administration. The IPL has grown into a multi-billion-dollar franchise since his departure, and the league's governance has evolved substantially under the BCCI's direct oversight.
